extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers (student journalists) with little or no previous journalism or photography experience
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step classroom-friendly guide to making environmental portraits (especially with a smartphone) for profile stories, covering composition, shoot planning, subject interaction, selection, editing, captions and ethics. Designed for students entering a profile/photo contest or learning photojournalism basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental portrait (definition and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: An environmental portrait includes the person’s surroundings or environment; the location, the lighting, the angle and the items included within the frame all provide readers with vital visual clues about the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the environment to reveal personality, background, work, hobbies or passions. Compare guesses about a subject from the photo with the profile text. Consider pose, expression, clothing, cropping, camera angle, eye direction, lighting, framing, items in the photo, and the setting as clues. Activity: select images and list inferences and the photo clues that led to them; judge how well the image foreshadows tone or content of the profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of thirds
rubrics_metrics.description: Place subjects away from center; imagine a tic-tac-toe grid and place the subject near one of the intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In portrait photography, aim to align the subject’s eyes along one of the grid lines or intersection points. Avoid centering the subject’s head/eyes in the middle which can cause viewers to miss surrounding storytelling details. Use camera grid feature to compose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle (including worm’s-eye and bird’s-eye)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach the subject from angles other than eye level to influence perceived power or vulnerability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worm’s-eye (shoot from below) can make a subject look bigger or more powerful; crouch or lie down for effect. Bird’s-eye (shoot from above) can make a subject look diminutive or imply power over them; use an elevated surface. Try straight-on, high, and low angles to tell the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of field (shallow vs wide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth of field describes how much of the background is in sharp focus; shallow depth of field keeps subject sharp and background blurred, wide depth of field keeps most of the scene in focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose shallow depth to focus attention on the subject while giving ambience; choose wide depth when background details are important to the story. On smartphones, consider portrait mode but decide how much background detail you need; avoid overusing portrait mode if background info matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leading lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Use natural or implied lines in the environment to lead the viewer’s eye toward the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for traffic lanes, architecture, paths, or the direction of a subject’s gaze. Place the subject where lines direct or intersect to emphasize them; this often complements rule of thirds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subframing (use of natural frames)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a natural frame within the scene—doorways, windows, trees, shadows, landscape elements—to accentuate the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subframe adds contextual information about the setting and directs attention to the subject. Notice and exploit architectural elements, bodies, or shadows for framing opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance (wide, midrange, close-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture subjects from varying distances—wide shots to set scene, midrange to establish subject, close-ups for intimate detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine photos of different distances to tell a fuller story (e.g., wide shot shows environment, midrange establishes person, close-up shows job or emotions). Use distance intentionally in a photo sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zoom with your feet (avoid digital zoom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pinching/using digital zoom on smartphone cameras because it enlarges pixels and causes pixelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move physically closer to your subject to frame the shot instead of using digital zoom to preserve image quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus and portrait mode use
rubrics_metrics.description: Tap on your subject on the smartphone screen to set focus; many phones have portrait mode which keeps subject sharp and softens the background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how much of the background is key to the story before using portrait mode. Use focus tap and available modes thoughtfully; do not let portrait mode obscure important contextual details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose using grid and camera orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use camera grid (nine-square) to apply rule of thirds and consider taking both vertical and horizontal shots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activate grid in camera settings to place eyes near intersections. Try both portrait (vertical) and landscape (horizontal) framing; choose the orientation that tells the most complete story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighting and exposure (make the most of natural light)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use natural light when possible; natural light is generally softer and more flattering than indoor fluorescents. Light should be in front of, not behind, your subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shoot during morning or late afternoon for inviting light. Indoors, use window or doorway light; if adding light, use soft bulbs or diffuse artificial light. Adjust smartphone exposure (iPhone: tap then slider; Android: use overflow/exposure buttons) to increase/decrease brightness as needed. Avoid backlighting unless purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice: take many shots and vary composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Take multiple shots when changing subject position, angle, or lighting; practice first with objects, then people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shooting digital means infinite frames—experiment with angles, distances, and compositions. Attend events or shoot on location to develop an eye. Activity: practice with a toy, then a willing friend or family member.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-shoot planning and visual concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the shoot, determine the focus of the profile and the visual concept—what story you want the photographs to tell and what they should feel like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the reporter’s story or interview the subject to learn what to emphasize. Decide what photographs (style, technique, medium) best suit the story—for instance, using tintypes for historical/nostalgic tone. Choose locations that reveal the subject’s life or work and avoid staged, empty-day settings that mask real activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing specific shoot locations and framing during shoot
rubrics_metrics.description: On location, think about framing, composition, lighting, and where to place the subject; move distracting items out of the shot and watch for awkward background elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scout the environment before the subject arrives, consider where light hits the face, and ensure nothing appears to be sticking out of the subject’s head. Take some photos of the empty environment for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the subject comfortable and directing without touching
rubrics_metrics.description: Build rapport, talk with the subject to relax them, and continue photographing while conversing; direct with gestures and verbal cues but do not touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about meaningful places, find common ground, ask subject to move rather than touch. Capture candid moments during conversation (thinking, laughing) rather than forcing expressions. Be in charge and give clear directions when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling the person’s story through details and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Think in terms of multiple photographs: sense of place, details, close-ups, actions—capture expressions or actions that reveal character and job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include detail shots (hands doing craft, tools) and sequences that balance environment and intimacy. Use compositional techniques like angle, depth, and distance to emphasize personality and role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping photographs interesting (try unfamiliar methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately try to make photographs in ways you’re not used to—change sides, try new angles, and experiment with light and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move around frequently during the shoot, take unexpected angles, and test how light plays from different positions to find compelling images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for profile photos
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting one to three photos for a profile, include at least one photo that clearly shows the subject’s face and consider distance and tone across selections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose images that together tell the story: a wide shot for environment, a midrange for subject, and a close-up for intimacy or detail. Consider tone (serious, lighthearted, inspiring, gritty) and how lighting, colors and expression contribute. If submitting to the Profile Contest, include 1–3 photos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing limits and photojournalism ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing should enhance quality but must not alter the reality of the photo; keep digital manipulation and postprocessing to a minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible edits: cropping, adjusting brightness, balancing colors—similar to darkroom corrections. Do not use filter effects, collages, or alter content. Submit photos as individual images. Review The New York Times Guidelines on Integrity and avoid manipulative edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cropping and aspect ratio guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Crop carefully in environmental portraits because every part of the picture is important; use standard aspect ratios to ensure fit with publication guides or frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate space that doesn’t help tell the story and cut distracting background information. Use standard ratios such as 1:1, 7:5, 4:3, 16:9 when cropping to fit common layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editing tools thoughtfully (apps and built-ins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Smartphone and desktop editing tools can adjust exposure, contrast, shadows, highlights, and sharpness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use built-in camera tools for grid, exposure, and basic edits; apps like Snapseed and Lightroom Mobile offer more options but should be used to enhance authenticity rather than to manipulate reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions: include the Five W’s and non-obvious context
rubrics_metrics.description: A caption should usually include who, what, when, where and why; explain storytelling details not obvious from the image and omit the obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make captions concise but informative—use them to convey what readers cannot see (e.g., what a technician is doing). For contest/lesson activity, add a one-sentence caption to each selected photo explaining the image.
